meta.title: Lawn mowing in Burton, MI | Grand Scapes
meta.description: Grand Scapes mows Burton, MI lawns weekly: mowed, trimmed, edged and blown off, timed to slow spring ground and finished clean along the ditches and walks.

hero.title: Weekly cuts, **straight lines.**
hero.lede: Grand Scapes mows Burton lawns on a set day each week: cut, trimmed along the house and fences, edged at the walk and drive, and blown off before we leave. Clean stripes in the grass and no clippings left on the concrete.

local.title: Established lawns on **slow ground.**
local.intro: Most lawns here were seeded around homes built in the 1950s and 60s, on loam the USDA rates somewhat poorly drained. The grass is settled and thick where it gets sun, the ground stays soft after a rain, and a lot of streets run a ditch where you might expect a curb. Each of those changes how a weekly cut should go.

points.title: Soft ground after rain
points.body: Conover loam, the most common soil in Burton, holds water. MSU Extension warns that turning a mower on saturated ground can pack the soil and tear the turf, so on a wet week we widen the turns and leave the soggy corner for last.

points.title: Ditches instead of curbs
points.body: Plenty of Burton streets drain to an open ditch. We mow the bank where the slope and footing allow it, trim the rest by hand, and keep clippings out of the ditch line so the water still has somewhere to go.

points.title: Mow high, take a third
points.body: MSU Extension puts current home lawn heights between 2 and 3.75 inches and says never to cut more than a third of the blade at once. In a fast May that can mean a lawn wants more than a weekly visit, and we will tell you if yours does.

points.title: A yard that gets away from you
points.body: The city handles overgrown yards on a complaint basis, with a ten day notice before a ticket or a city cleanup billed to the owner. A standing weekly cut keeps that letter out of your mailbox, even in a month you are out of town.

logistics.title: How weekly mowing runs in Burton.
body: Rob comes out first, walks the lawn with you and quotes the season. Once you say go, you get a set day, and the crew shows up on it every week with zero turn mowers, trimmers and blowers on the trailer.

Every visit follows one routine: mow, trim around the house, beds, trees and fences, edge the walks and the drive, then blow the hard surfaces clean. Clippings go back onto the lawn, which MSU Extension recommends because they break down fast and do not cause thatch.

When the yard also needs a [spring cleanup](/spring-cleanup-burton-mi/) or [leaf removal](/leaf-removal-burton-mi/), the same crew handles it, so one call covers the season from the first cut to the last.

faq.q: Do you mow lawns in Burton, MI?
faq.a: Yes. Grand Scapes mows residential lawns in Burton every week on a set day. Each visit includes mowing, trimming, edging and blowing off the walks and drive. Rob comes out to see the lawn and quotes it for free.

faq.q: How high should I mow my lawn in Michigan?
faq.a: MSU Extension puts current home lawn standards between 2 and 3.75 inches, and says taller grass shades the soil and holds back crabgrass. The bigger rule is never to remove more than a third of the blade in one cut. We set the deck to the lawn and the season.

faq.q: Can you mow the ditch in front of my house?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Many Burton streets drain to an open ditch, and we mow the bank where the slope and footing allow, then trim what a mower should not reach. Clippings stay out of the ditch so it can carry water.

Most weeks, no. MSU Extension says clippings do not add to thatch and should go back on the lawn when no more than a third is cut at a time. When the grass gets ahead in a wet spring, or leaves start falling, we bag as the yard needs it.

faq.q: What happens if my lawn gets too tall in Burton?
faq.a: The city works overgrown yards on a complaint basis. A valid complaint brings a ten day notice, and if nothing changes the owner can be ticketed or billed for a city cleanup. A weekly cut keeps it from ever getting that far.
